extracted.intended_audience: newspaper cub reporters, novice reporters, and journalism students
extracted.subtask_description: Practical newsroom guidance for producing 'clean copy' and behaving effectively in a newspaper office: how to prepare, label, and correct copy; master the style sheet; learn the town and paper; and demonstrate the habits editors value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clean copy
rubrics_metrics.description: Copy should be neat, legible, and free of scrawled penciled-in corrections and excessive insertions; clean copy suggests thoroughness and care, while dirty copy suggests slovenliness and carelessness about facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors judge reporters by the cleanness of their copy; clean copy goes through the editing desk more easily and is less likely to be decimated. If copy is messy, the desk may cut most of it rather than laboriously revise it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correcting longhand changes carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: When making longhand corrections, cross out errant words carefully and mark the correct versions neatly above them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If such amendments are many, recopy the story — it takes only a few moments. Messy corrections leave no room for the copy editor and impede editing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfect typing (accuracy first)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters should perfect their typing rapidly, emphasizing accuracy and allowing speed to follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poor typewriting is a common cause of dirty copy. The habit of good typing forms quickly and endures; whichever habit (accurate or erratic) is established will stick.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish confusing handwritten letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Carefully distinguish between letters that are easily mistaken (a and o, m and w, n and u).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prevent mistakes, overscore some letters and underscore others so corrections and notes are unambiguous when read by copy editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reorder paragraphs by cutting and pasting, not messy marks
rubrics_metrics.description: When changing paragraph sequence, cut the story apart and paste it together in the desired order rather than trying to shift paragraphs by messy direction-indicating lines or arrows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This keeps copy clean and readable for editors — avoid 'mussy direction-indicating lines' that make editing difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be meticulous ('spinsterish') about copy presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a punctilious attitude toward the physical presentation of copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meticulousness in presentation signals professionalism and helps editors; casual or sloppy presentation invites harsh treatment and reduced assignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper slugging/labeling of copy
rubrics_metrics.description: Each story must be tagged or 'slugged' to show where it should go in the paper, who wrote it, and any special information editors need; put this information in the upper left corner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Labeling should state appropriate page/section (page 1, city page, suburban) and any particulars (exclusive, contains new matter, of special interest to certain editions). Mis-tagging (e.g., failing to mark '1st Ed.') can cause the story to miss an edition or be edited too late.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leave space for headline and editor notes
rubrics_metrics.description: After the slugline in the upper left corner, drop four or five inches down before beginning the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This leaves the copy editor ample space for writing the headline or adding directions; failing to leave space complicates editing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know and mark appropriate edition(s)
rubrics_metrics.description: Know which geographic or timed editions exist and mark copy for the edition(s) to which the story applies (e.g., '1st Ed.', 'All Eds.').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't overclaim 'All Eds.' — editors will cut and punish stories improperly labeled. Verify which edition would find the story interesting and label accordingly to avoid late editing or loss of placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify names and facts especially for wide-edition stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Before labeling a story for many editions, verify dozens of names and other factual details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A story marked 'All Eds.' with many unverified names invites exhaustive correction, patching, and rewriting by editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mark stories 'With Cut' and describe picture details
rubrics_metrics.description: If a story carries a picture, mark it 'With Cut' and indicate what the picture is about and how many columns wide it will be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without this warning the story may go into type and later require page rebuilding when the engraving arrives; failure to mark 'With Cut' causes extra work for make-up and composing rooms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include an end-mark to show story completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Each story must carry an end-mark to indicate it is complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copy unmarked as complete can be set aside awaiting the rest, then forgotten, creating snarls in both the editing desk and composing room and causing editors to search for missing fragments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master the style sheet
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn the paper's style sheet — the authoritative list of preferences in spelling, punctuation, capitalization, abbreviation, and other stylistic points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The style sheet creates uniformity, helping readers and editors. Study grouped rules (punctuation, abbreviations), memorize examples and notable exceptions, and note whether the paper uses up style, down style, or moderate down style. Rapid mastery impresses copy editors and improves prospects for advancement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand style-sheet groupings and exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice the major characteristics/trends of the style sheet (capitalization and abbreviation practices) and its exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Style sheets often contain historical compromises and exceptions; begin by learning rules you already practice, then focus on unfamiliar or exceptional directions and their examples to recall them quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn the town (local geography and sources)
rubrics_metrics.description: Know the city's geography, transit, location of fire/police stations, key businesses, churches and ministers, prominent professionals, hotels and what customers they attract, and other local specifics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compile lists of names and addresses, study directories and classified listings, and learn which locations or hotels suit particular sources. This saves time, reveals story leads/specials, and impresses the city editor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate resourcefulness and initiative
rubrics_metrics.description: Show initiative by finding unusual sources and unassigned stories (e.g., locating a 'diver' in the telephone directory inland).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors praise reporters who 'didn't know we had one of those fellows in town' — such discoveries earn better, livelier assignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the paper's policy, background, and personalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn the paper's editorial policies, its friends and enemies, and the preferences of the publisher and other key figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This knowledge prevents inadvertent offense, informs judgment about what to pursue or avoid, helps get the right sources quickly, and is gained through experience and repeated exposure to policy questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be patient; stay to learn (apprenticeship/tenure advice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan to remain with a first paper for at least two to three years to become fully seasoned and valuable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It takes time to experience the gamut of assignments, learn policy and personalities, and acquire the initiative to act without asking questions. Editors often expect at least a year or more before offering higher pay or responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize good ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalism education should emphasize good ethics and an appeal to unselfishness to encourage loyalty and professionalism among graduates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethics training helps retain staff and produces reporters who remain fair and trustworthy as they gain experience; city editors value ethical behavior when investing in training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sloppy practices that burden editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid behaviors (poor slugging, failing to mark 'With Cut' or end-mark, messy corrections, unverified names, lazy use of 'All Eds.') that create extra work for desk, make-up, and composing rooms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such anti-patterns invite chastisement, reduced assignments, and make a reporter appear inexperienced or careless; learning office procedures demonstrates competence and reduces friction.
